The worker still completes every task as READY (StubGenerator's placeholder GLBs pass all validators), so real designers' products get served empty box-mesh 3D previews in production with only an INFO-level startup log line (`Model provider: StubGenerator`) as the sole signal — no WARN/ERROR, and docker-compose.prod.yml itself encodes the same silent default (`MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER: ${MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER:-mock}`, line 67).
advisory.fix: Have `prod_deploy.sh setup`/`up` warn loudly (or refuse to proceed) if `MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER`/`AVATAR_GENERATION_PROVIDER`/`RIGGING_PROVIDER` are still `mock` when `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`/an explicit `--prod` flag indicates a production run; at minimum, log a `logger.warning(...)` (not `info`) in main.py whenever a provider resolves to its stub/mock branch via the default rather than an explicit, recognized value.

advisory.title: RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender is a documented, selectable option but neither worker image installs the Blender binary it requires
advisory.proof: .env.example (lines 89-92) and CLAUDE.md both document `RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender` as a valid option requiring `BLENDER_PATH` (default `blender`, main.py line 79). Neither worker/Dockerfile nor worker/Dockerfile.rigging installs a `blender` package or binary (Dockerfile.rigging's apt-get list is only `gcc g++ cmake git`). `BlenderRiggingProvider.generate()` (providers/blender_rigging_provider.py) invokes `self.blender_path` via `subprocess` — with no `blender` executable on PATH in either image, every rigging task fails at runtime with a `FileNotFoundError`-class error the first time this provider is selected in a containerized deployment. It degrades gracefully (task FAILED, not a crash), but an operator who toggles `RIGGING_PROVIDER=blender` expecting the documented behavior gets 100% rigging-task failures with no earlier validation.
advisory.fix: Either install Blender in a dedicated image for this provider (document it as container-unsupported otherwise), or remove/clearly flag `blender` as host-only/unsupported-in-Docker in .env.example and CLAUDE.md so operators don't select it expecting it to work in the shipped containers.

advisory.title: Missing .dockerignore — COPY . . bakes local dev artifacts (.venv, __pycache__, .pytest_cache, tests/) into the image when present in the build context
advisory.proof: No `.dockerignore` exists in worker/ or at the repo root (confirmed via `ls`). Both worker/Dockerfile (line 10) and worker/Dockerfile.rigging (line 17) do `COPY . .` against the `./worker` build context. On this checkout, `worker/` currently contains `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, and `.pytest_cache/` directories alongside the real source; without an ignore file, any `docker compose build`/`./prod_deploy.sh update` run from a working tree in that state (e.g. a deploy host also used for local testing, or a CI runner that doesn't clean between steps) copies all of it into the final image layer, inflating image size and build time and risking accidental inclusion of local-only virtualenv/cache contents in what ships to production.
advisory.fix: Add a worker/.dockerignore excluding at minimum `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `.pytest_cache/`, `tests/`, and any `*.pyc`.

advisory.title: No resource limits anywhere in docker-compose.prod.yml — a torch-laden worker runs unbounded next to an uncapped JVM on the same host
advisory.proof: docker-compose.prod.yml's single `worker` service builds from `Dockerfile.rigging`, which installs worker/requirements.txt (torch, smplx, trimesh — unconditional deps, not feature-gated) plus libigl + robust-laplacian on top — the heaviest possible worker image, always running in prod regardless of which providers are actually enabled. Dev splits this into a base `worker` and a separate, capped `rigging-worker` (docker-compose.yml lines 105-109: `deploy: resources: limits: memory: 1G, cpus: '2.0'`), but prod has no such limit on its single merged worker, nor on any other service. The dev-only `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-Xmx384m -Xms128m"` (docker-compose.yml line 43) is also absent from the prod server block, so the JVM heap sizes itself off whatever memory the host reports with no explicit ceiling. On a modest single-host production VM, a real avatar/rigging task running concurrently with normal traffic can consume unbounded memory and trigger the OOM killer against mysql/server, which (per the restart-policy finding above) will not auto-recover.
advisory.fix: Add `deploy.resources.limits` (memory/cpu) to every service in docker-compose.prod.yml sized to the target host, and re-introduce an explicit JVM heap bound for the server container.

advisory.title: No backup mechanism is wired into the production deployment tooling
advisory.proof: prod_deploy.sh's command dispatch covers setup/up/update/ssl-init/ssl-renew/health/logs/stop only — there is no `backup` or `db` subcommand, and docker-compose.prod.yml defines no backup/cron sidecar either. dev.sh does have a working pair (`db backup` runs `mysqldump -u iyae -p"${DB_PASSWORD}" iyae > backup_${timestamp}.sql`), but it targets the dev compose project and is never referenced from the prod script. If the `mysql_data` volume is lost or corrupted in production (disk failure, accidental `docker volume rm`, a bad migration), there is no documented or scripted recovery path for user accounts, orders, or Stripe payment metadata.
advisory.fix: Add a `backup`/`restore` command to prod_deploy.sh (or a scheduled mysqldump sidecar in docker-compose.prod.yml) before go-live.

advisory.title: add_header inheritance trap drops the three security headers on /uploads/, /assets/, and /_next/static
advisory.proof: nginx only inherits `add_header` directives from a parent context into a child context when the child defines none of its own. `location /uploads/` (line 38), `location /assets/` (line 44), and `location /_next/static` (line 50) each define their own `add_header Cache-Control ...`, which silently drops the server-level `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, and `Referrer-Policy` headers (lines 13-15) for every response served from those three locations -- only `/api/` and `/` (which define no add_header of their own) actually get the security headers. `/uploads/` is exactly where designer-submitted product images land, and `server/src/main/java/com/iyae/service/FileStorageService.java` validates uploads only by the client-supplied multipart `Content-Type` header (never the actual file bytes/magic numbers) before writing the content to a `.jpg/.png/.webp` file -- so this is the one location serving attacker-influenced bytes that is missing `nosniff`. I could not fully confirm current mainstream browsers would content-sniff a `Content-Type: image/jpeg` response (nginx derives that from the `.jpg` extension via its own mime map, not from the uploader) into an HTML/script execution context, so I'm not asserting a proven XSS chain -- only the concrete, verifiable nginx misconfiguration that removes the intended defense-in-depth header exactly where it would matter most.
advisory.fix: Move the three security `add_header` directives into a reusable snippet (e.g. `include security-headers.conf;`) and include it explicitly inside /uploads/, /assets/, and /_next/static as well, so they coexist with the Cache-Control header instead of being silently discarded. Separately, make FileStorageService validate actual image bytes (e.g. via a lightweight magic-number/image-decoder check) instead of trusting the client-declared Content-Type.

advisory.title: No tuned proxy timeouts for /api/, while AI chat calls to external providers have no explicit HTTP client timeout either
advisory.proof: The /api/ location sets no `proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_connect_timeout`/`proxy_send_timeout`, so nginx uses its compiled-in 60s defaults for every call through it, including `POST /api/chat/sessions/{id}/messages`, which synchronously calls an external AI provider (Claude/DeepSeek/MiniMax per server/CLAUDE.md). A grep of server/src/main/java/com/iyae/ai/*.java found no `timeout`/`Duration.of` configuration on those HTTP clients, so a slow provider response can run well past nginx's 60s ceiling. When that happens, nginx returns a bare 504 to the user (an opaque failure rather than a clear 'AI is slow, retry' message) while the Spring thread handling that request keeps blocking on the still-in-flight AI call; repeated slow responses under concurrent chat usage tie up request threads with no corresponding client signal.
advisory.fix: Set an explicit, generous `proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_send_timeout` (e.g. 90-120s) scoped to /api/chat/ specifically (or /api/ generally if other calls can also be slow), and add an explicit timeout to the AI provider HTTP clients that is shorter than the nginx timeout so the server fails fast and returns a clean error/fallback instead of nginx cutting the connection first.

advisory.title: No edge-level rate or connection limiting anywhere in nginx; only a 10-route in-app allowlist is throttled
advisory.proof: Neither nginx.conf nor conf.d/default.conf contains any `limit_req_zone`/`limit_req`/`limit_conn_zone`/`limit_conn` directive (confirmed by reading both files in full) -- the edge imposes no per-IP request-rate or connection-count ceiling on any path. The only throttling anywhere in the stack is `RateLimitFilter`, an explicit allowlist of exactly 10 route patterns (login, register, forgot/reset-password-adjacent, chat POSTs, checkout, public avatar generate, avatar delete, recommended-size). Every other path -- full product catalog browse/search, and the unauthenticated static locations /assets/ and /uploads/ -- has zero rate limiting at any layer. I could not confirm this causes resource exhaustion under normal (non-adversarial) load specifically, since that depends on host sizing and real traffic volume that isn't visible from the code; the confirmed fact is the structural absence of any edge-level limiter, which stacks with the unauthenticated avatar-enumeration finding above (nothing throttles that scan either).
advisory.fix: Add `limit_req_zone`/`limit_conn_zone` in nginx.conf keyed on $binary_remote_addr with a generous global ceiling (defense-in-depth beneath the app-level limiter), and specifically rate-limit /assets/ and /uploads/ given they currently have no protection at all.

advisory.title: prod_deploy.sh health check reports Docker 'unhealthy' containers as OK
advisory.fix: Don't substring-match the human-readable Status column. Use `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <container>` and compare for an exact `healthy`, so a container whose own HEALTHCHECK is failing is reported as an error instead of OK.

advisory.title: dev.sh 'reset' wipes all Docker volumes with zero confirmation
advisory.evidence:
reset)
    docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" down -v
    echo "All data wiped."
    ;;
advisory.fix: Add the same interactive confirmation pattern already used by `db restore` (or require an explicit --yes flag) before running `down -v`, since this one command destroys the MySQL data volume and all generated 3D assets irrecoverably.

advisory.title: 'db restore' confirmation prompt doesn't validate input, so it's a no-op gate
advisory.evidence:
warn "This will overwrite the current database. Press Enter to continue or Ctrl+C to cancel."
      read -r
advisory.fix: Require the operator to type a specific confirmation token (e.g. the environment name, or literal "yes") and compare it before proceeding, instead of accepting any stdin content (including a blank line piped in non-interactively, e.g. echo | ./dev.sh db restore f.sql).

advisory.title: DB password passed as a mysqldump/mysql CLI argument (visible via ps/docker top)
advisory.evidence:
docker compose -f "$COMPOSE_FILE" exec -T mysql \
        mysqldump -u iyae -p"${DB_PASSWORD}" iyae > "$backup_file"
advisory.fix: Pass the password via the MYSQL_PWD environment variable to the exec'd process (docker compose exec -T -e MYSQL_PWD="${DB_PASSWORD}" mysql mysqldump -u iyae iyae ...) instead of -p"${DB_PASSWORD}" on argv, so it isn't visible in the container's process list for the duration of the command. The same pattern is repeated in the db restore branch (mysql -u iyae -p"${DB_PASSWORD}").

advisory.title: .env and DB backup dumps are created with default (world-readable) permissions
advisory.proof: Verified host umask is 022, so cp .env.example .env (dev.sh line 131, and the identical pattern in prod_deploy.sh's setup) produces a 644, world-readable .env with no follow-up chmod. That file ends up holding DB_PASSWORD, JWT_SECRET, ANTHROPIC/DEEPSEEK/MINIMAX/WORKER_*_API_KEY, INTERNAL_MAIL_SECRET and RESEND_API_KEY. The db backup mysqldump redirect (> "$backup_file") has the same gap — the resulting SQL dump (full user table incl. password hashes and PII) also lands world-readable in the repo working directory. Any other local account on a shared dev/build host can read both files.
advisory.fix: Add chmod 600 .env immediately after it is created/modified in both dev.sh's cmd_setup/generate_jwt_secret and prod_deploy.sh's setup/generate_jwt_secret, and chmod 600 "$backup_file" immediately after the mysqldump redirect in cmd_db backup.

advisory.title: No explicit `permissions:` block — GITHUB_TOKEN runs at repo-default scope, not least-privilege
advisory.proof: No job or workflow-level `permissions:` key exists anywhere in the file (confirmed by grep across all 293 lines). None of the current steps write to the repo/PRs/packages, so there is no live sink today, but the token inherits whatever the repository's default Actions permission setting is (which can be read-write) rather than being pinned down. If a future step is added (e.g. a PR comment step, a release step) it would silently inherit broader-than-needed scope.
advisory.fix: Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of the workflow (the only elevated need, if any, is `actions: read`/`checks: write` for artifact upload, which does not require extra scope); add narrower per-job overrides only where a job genuinely needs more.

advisory.title: All third-party actions pinned to mutable version tags, not commit SHAs
advisory.proof: Every action in the file (actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-node@v4, actions/setup-java@v4, actions/setup-python@v5, actions/upload-artifact@v4, gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4) is referenced by a floating major-version tag. If any of these tags were ever repointed to a malicious commit (the tj-actions/changed-files incident in March 2025 showed this happens to real, previously-trusted actions), the next `push`-to-main or PR run would execute attacker code with whatever token/secret scope the job has, with no diff for a human to review.
advisory.fix: Pin each `uses:` to a full commit SHA with the version as a trailing comment (e.g. `actions/checkout@<sha> # v4.2.2`), and use Dependabot/Renovate to keep the pinned SHAs current.

advisory.title: No dependency, SAST, or secret-scanning job anywhere in CI
advisory.evidence:
- name: Unit tests
        working-directory: web
        run: npm run test
advisory.proof: The four jobs (web-unit, server-tests, worker-tests, playwright) only typecheck/lint/test; grepping the whole file for audit/codeql/snyk/trivy/gitleaks/bandit/safety/semgrep returns no hits. A newly-introduced vulnerable npm/pip/gradle dependency, or an accidentally committed credential, would merge to main and reach production with no automated check catching it before release.
advisory.fix: Add an `npm audit --audit-level=high` step to web-unit, a `pip-audit`/`safety` step to worker-tests, a Gradle dependency-check (or OWASP dependency-check plugin) step to server-tests, and a standalone secret-scanning job (gitleaks/trufflehog) run on every push and PR.

advisory.title: Production worker image and production Spring/nginx topology are never built or exercised by CI
advisory.evidence: run: docker compose up -d --build mysql server web
advisory.proof: Verified against docker-compose.prod.yml and worker/Dockerfile.rigging: production's `worker` service builds `worker/Dockerfile.rigging` (apt-get gcc/g++/cmake + pip-installed libigl/robust-laplacian), and production runs `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` behind an nginx reverse proxy. The Playwright job explicitly limits the build to `mysql server web` using the dev compose file and the dev Spring profile; worker-tests installs Python deps directly via pip, never through either Dockerfile. A break in the apt/pip toolchain of Dockerfile.rigging, or a prod-profile-only misconfiguration, would not be caught by any CI job — only discovered when `prod_deploy.sh up` is run against a real deploy.
advisory.fix: Add a CI step that runs `docker compose build worker rigging-worker` (or builds Dockerfile.rigging directly) so the production worker image is validated, and consider a periodic/scheduled job that brings up docker-compose.prod.yml with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod to catch prod-only config drift before a real release.

advisory.title: ResaleService JSON snapshot parsing swallows exceptions with no logging, silently emptying a buyer's resale eligibility and purchase-provenance checks
advisory.proof: parseSnapshot() feeds listEligibleItems() (what a buyer can resell) and findOwningOrderId() (the ownership gate createListing() relies on to accept/reject a resale listing). If any order's itemsSnapshot JSON fails to deserialize into SnapshotItem — e.g. a future field rename/type change, or a historical row written before a schema change — every call site degrades silently and identically to 'the user owns nothing': listEligibleItems returns an empty list (buyer sees 'you have nothing to resell' instead of a transient/real error) and createListing throws the ordinary user-facing 'You can only resell items you've purchased' (IllegalArgumentException), which looks exactly like a legitimate rejection rather than a parsing bug. Because there is no log statement in either catch block (unlike every analogous parse-failure handler elsewhere in the server codebase), there is also no way to detect this regression after the fact short of a user complaint.
advisory.fix: Log at warn/error with the order id and exception before returning List.of(), mirroring the sibling pattern used everywhere else in this codebase (e.g. GenerationService.extractField, AvatarService.extractField, OutfitService.parseJsonList all log a warning on parse failure). Consider surfacing a degraded-state signal (e.g. a counter/metric) rather than a bare empty list, since an empty result here is indistinguishable from 'user legitimately owns nothing.'

advisory.title: No graceful shutdown anywhere (Spring default is immediate, no stop_grace_period) and the Stripe webhook silently ACKs a session with no Order row
advisory.proof: There is no `server.shutdown: graceful` and no `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` in `application.yml`, `application-prod.yml` or `application-dev.yml` (grepped `shutdown|graceful` across `server/src/main/resources/` and `config/` — only `SchedulerConfig`'s `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` exists, which covers the @Scheduled pool, not HTTP requests), and `docker-compose.prod.yml` sets no `stop_grace_period`. So `prod_deploy.sh update` → `docker compose up -d` sends SIGTERM and Tomcat drops in-flight requests at once. The costly window is `CheckoutService.initiateCheckout`: the Stripe session is created at line 131 and the `Order` row is only committed at line 151 (`txTemplate.executeWithoutResult`). A SIGTERM between the two leaves a live, payable Stripe session with no order; the buyer pays, and `fulfillPaidSession` does `orderRepository.findByStripeSessionId(session.getId()).ifPresent(...)` (line 214) — no row, no log, controller returns 200, so Stripe never retries. Money taken, no order, cart not cleared, nothing recorded. I could not confirm how long a deploy's SIGTERM window actually is in practice, but the ordering of the two writes is in the code.
advisory.fix: Set `server.shutdown: graceful` plus `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s`, add `stop_grace_period: 40s` to the server service, and make the unknown-session branch of `fulfillPaidSession` log an error and return a non-2xx so Stripe retries instead of silently dropping it.

advisory.title: User email addresses are logged at INFO on every transactional email and on checkout failures
advisory.evidence: log.info("{} email sent via Resend to {}", type, toEmail);
advisory.proof: `application-prod.yml` sets `root: INFO` / `com.iyae: INFO`, so this fires for every registration and every password reset. The same pattern appears in `AuthMailService:121` (`Failed to send {} email via Resend to {}`), `CheckoutService:159/162` (`Stripe session creation failed for user {}`, with `email`), `CheckoutService:361` (`...stub order {} for user {}`, with `user.getEmail()`) and `OutfitService:93/312/428/430` (`for user={}` with `user.getEmail()`). Combined with the unrotated default `json-file` driver (no `logging:` block in either compose file), a full roster of customer email addresses accumulates indefinitely on the host and in whatever log shipper is attached later — a GDPR/PIPEDA exposure that also means anyone with `docker logs` access, including a future CI/monitoring integration, gets the customer list. I did not find passwords, tokens or body measurements being logged.
advisory.fix: Log `user.getId()` instead of the email everywhere (the `AuthService` sites already do this correctly — e.g. `AuthService:155` `for user {}` with `user.getId()`), and configure log rotation + retention on all prod containers.

advisory.title: No connection-pool, thread-pool or container resource sizing in production, and one worker container serializes all three task queues
advisory.proof: Grepping `hikari|tomcat|max-connections|threads` across `server/src/main/resources/` returns nothing, so production runs HikariCP defaults (maximumPoolSize 10, connectionTimeout 30s) behind Tomcat defaults (200 request threads) against a stock `mysql:8.0` (max_connections 151) that is given no `command:` tuning in `docker-compose.prod.yml`. Under load the 191 threads that cannot get a connection block for a full 30s before failing, which nginx (default `proxy_read_timeout 60s`) happily waits on — and the three `fixedDelay = 5000` materializer tasks plus the resale sweeper compete for the same 10 connections. Separately the prod `worker` processes model, avatar and rigging tasks sequentially in one loop (`worker/main.py:138/175/210`), so a multi-minute rigging job stalls avatar generation for every buyer in the queue; and unlike the dev `rigging-worker` (`docker-compose.yml:105-109`, 1G/2 CPU limit) the prod worker has no `deploy.resources.limits`, so a rigging OOM can push the kernel OOM killer onto MySQL. I did not load-test this, so the exhaustion point is inferred from the defaults rather than measured. The JDBC URL also disables TLS to MySQL (`useSSL=false`) — contained to the Docker network, but it means DB traffic is cleartext.
advisory.fix: Set `spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size`/`connection-timeout` and `server.tomcat.threads.max` explicitly and size them against MySQL's `max_connections`; add `proxy_connect_timeout`/`proxy_read_timeout`/`proxy_send_timeout` to the nginx `/api/` location; add memory/CPU limits to the prod worker; and split rigging into its own container in prod as the dev compose already does.

advisory.title: Paid Stripe session with no matching order is silently acknowledged
advisory.proof: `fulfillPaidSession` uses `ifPresent` with no `else`, and the controller returns 200 unconditionally, so a `checkout.session.completed` whose `stripe_session_id` has no row produces no log, no metric, and no Stripe retry. That is the correct outcome for events belonging to another environment sharing the Stripe account, but it is indistinguishable from a genuinely lost order (order row never committed after session creation, or deleted), and `orders.stripe_session_id` has no unique index (V9) to make the lookup authoritative. I could not construct a code path where the user obtains the session URL without the order row having been committed, so I am filing this as reliability/observability rather than confirmed money loss.
advisory.fix: Log at WARN (ideally with an alert metric) when a `paid` session has no matching order, and add a unique index on `orders.stripe_session_id` so the mapping is enforced by the database.

advisory.title: Webhook clears the user's whole current cart, not the purchased snapshot — items added after checkout started are silently deleted
advisory.proof: The order already carries an immutable `items_snapshot` of what was paid for, but fulfillment deletes every row in the cart. Two-things-at-once scenario: the user starts checkout in tab A, then in tab B adds two more items while the Stripe page is open; the webhook lands and wipes all cart rows, so the two unpaid items vanish with no notice. Bounded impact (lost cart state, not money), but it is silent and the data to do it correctly is already on the order.
advisory.fix: Delete only the cart rows matching the `(productId, selectedSize)` pairs in the order's `items_snapshot`, leaving anything added afterwards in place.

advisory.title: Model/avatar stale-reclaim has no attempt ceiling and can run a second generation for a task that is still live, writing the same output path
advisory.evidence:
UPDATE model_generation_tasks
                SET status = 'PENDING'
                WHERE status = 'RUNNING'
                  AND updated_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE
advisory.proof: Unlike `rigging_task_queue.claim_task` (which filters `attempt_count < %s`) and `rigging_task_queue.reclaim_stale_tasks` (which fails tasks at the attempt limit), the model and avatar queues neither cap attempts on claim nor on reclaim. A task whose provider call hangs past 15 minutes is therefore returned to PENDING forever: each cycle increments `attempt_count`, re-invokes the provider (for `MODEL_GENERATION_PROVIDER=meshy` that is ~30 paid credits per attempt, indefinitely), and never reaches a terminal FAILED state the designer can retry from — `GenerationService.getStatus` reports RUNNING/PENDING indefinitely. The reclaim also does not coordinate with the live worker: the original process is still running, and both it and the new claimant write `products/{product_id}/tasks/{task_id}/preview.glb` (same task id ⇒ same path), so the first to call `complete_task` (status is RUNNING again, so the guard passes) publishes READY while the other process is still writing the same file, and the server can materialize a `GarmentAsset` pointing at a partially written GLB.
advisory.fix: Mirror the rigging queue: filter `attempt_count < MAX_ATTEMPTS` in `claim_task`, and in `reclaim_stale_tasks` move tasks at/over the limit to FAILED instead of PENDING. Include a claim token (or `attempt_count`) in the `complete_task`/`fail_task` WHERE clause so a superseded worker cannot publish, and key the output path on the attempt as well as the task id.

advisory.title: Any authenticated user can reserve (and so hide) any resale listing for 30 minutes, with no rate limit on the resale checkout path
advisory.proof: `POST /api/resale/listings/{id}/checkout` reserves before any payment intent exists, and `ResaleService.browse` only returns `ResaleStatus.LISTED`, so a reservation removes the listing from the marketplace until the 30-minute TTL sweep. `RateLimitFilter`'s rule table matches the prefix `/api/checkout` (RateLimitFilter.java:37) — it does not match `/api/resale/...` — and there is no per-user cap on concurrent reservations. One authenticated account can therefore loop over `GET /api/resale/listings` and POST a checkout for every listing, re-running every 30 minutes, to keep the entire pre-loved marketplace invisible and unbuyable. Abuse-driven rather than normal-load, hence MEDIUM.
advisory.fix: Add a `RateRule("POST", "/api/resale/listings/", "/checkout", …)` to `RateLimitFilter`, cap the number of simultaneous RESERVED listings per buyer, and shorten the reservation TTL to match the Stripe session expiry set in the fix for the TTL finding.

advisory.title: `processReadyTasks` catches per-task failures inside one shared transaction, so the per-item isolation it implies does not exist
advisory.proof: The whole batch runs in one transaction while `materializeGarmentAsset` failures are swallowed per task (`catch (Exception e) { log.error(...) }`), which reads as "one bad task is skipped". For a JPA/constraint failure raised at flush, the Hibernate session is left unusable and the commit fails, so every task already materialized in that pass is rolled back while the only log line names a single task; `SchedulerConfig` then swallows the commit error too, and the scheduler re-attempts the same batch every 5 seconds — designers' 3D assets stop appearing with no clear signal. `RiggingService.processReadyTasks` has the identical shape (RiggingService.java:169-180). I could not pin a specific input that reliably throws inside `materializeGarmentAsset` on the current schema, so this is filed as misleading error handling rather than a confirmed outage.
advisory.fix: Make the loop non-transactional and move `@Transactional` onto a per-task method invoked through the bean proxy (or `REQUIRES_NEW`), so a failure isolates to that task; additionally guard materialization with a unique constraint on `garment_assets(product_id, …)` or an existence check so a retry cannot create duplicate asset rows.

advisory.title: Guest body measurements are stored indefinitely by unauthenticated callers with no deletion path and no retention job
advisory.proof: `POST /api/public/avatar/generate` is permitAll and requires no identity. `buildInputPayload` (lines 112-134) serialises `heightCm`, `weightKg`, `waistCm` (estimated from BMI when absent, line 118-121), `chestCm`, `hipsCm`, `shoulderWidthCm` and `inseamCm` into the row's `input_payload` JSON column (V6__avatar_generation_tasks.sql declares `input_payload JSON`). Those rows are never removed: `AvatarService.deleteAvatarData` is keyed on an authenticated principal's email (`deleteAvatarData(String email)`, AvatarService.java:142, reached only via `auth.getName()` in AvatarController.java:38), and no guest can authenticate as `guest@iyae.internal` — its password is a discarded random UUID (GuestAvatarService.java:87). SchedulerConfig declares no retention or pruning task of any kind (its only jobs are task materialisation, resale reservation expiry, and weather refresh). Result: an anonymous visitor who tries the landing-page avatar has their body measurements written to a production table permanently, with no self-service deletion, no admin tooling, and no expiry. I could not confirm any out-of-band retention process (cron, DB event) — none exists in the repository.
advisory.fix: Add a scheduled purge of `avatar_generation_tasks` rows belonging to the guest sentinel user older than a short, documented TTL (hours, not days), deleting the on-disk output alongside — `AvatarService.deleteAvatarFiles` already has the recursive-delete helper to reuse. State the TTL in the guest try-on UI.

advisory.title: Registration requires agreeing to a Terms and Privacy Policy that does not exist anywhere in the product
advisory.evidence: I agree to {BRAND.name}'s Terms and Privacy Policy.
advisory.proof: The consent checkbox is rendered as plain text with no link target. There is no `/privacy` or `/terms` route in `web/app/` (the directory listing contains neither), no file matching `*privacy*` or `*terms*` anywhere outside node_modules, and this is the single occurrence of the words "Privacy Policy" across web/app, web/components and web/lib. So a user collecting-consent flow asks 18-30 year olds to accept documents they cannot read, for a product that stores body measurements, gender identity, age range and a derived 3D body mesh. Separately, no surface discloses data handling at the point of collection: a grep for `third.party|we store|consent|anthropic|claude|deepseek|minimax|data deletion` across web/app/profile and web/components/profile returns nothing, and the avatar page's privacy copy is limited to "Permanently removes your 3D avatar and measurements." (web/app/profile/avatar/page.tsx:465).
advisory.fix: Ship a privacy policy and terms page (or external links) and wire the checkbox label to them, covering at minimum: what body measurements are collected, that a 3D body mesh is derived and stored, retention periods, and the deletion controls available. Add a one-line disclosure at the measurement-entry and avatar-generation points of collection.

advisory.title: No fast test validates that the JPA entity mappings match the real Flyway migrations (ddl-auto=validate in prod)
advisory.evidence:
hibernate:
      ddl-auto: create-drop
    ...
  flyway:
    enabled: false
advisory.proof: Every server test (including `IyaeApplicationTests`, which explicitly excludes `DataSourceAutoConfiguration`/`HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration`/`FlywayAutoConfiguration`) and every `@DataJpaTest` (e.g. `ResaleListingRepositoryDataJpaTest`) runs against H2 with Hibernate auto-generating the schema from entities and Flyway turned off — so none of them ever load the real V1-V21 migration SQL. Production uses `ddl-auto: validate` against Flyway-applied migrations (server/src/main/resources/application.yml:9), so a column type/nullability mismatch only surfaces as a boot failure once deployed. CLAUDE.md documents a real near-miss of exactly this class of bug (`PasswordResetTokenRepository.consumeToken` assigning CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to an Instant, "breaks full JPA bootstrap"). The only thing in CI that would currently catch a repeat is the Playwright job's `docker compose up` + health-check retry loop, which gives a generic 5-minute timeout with no indication the root cause is a schema mismatch.
advisory.fix: Add a dedicated, fast test (or Gradle task) that boots Spring Boot against a real database (e.g. Testcontainers MySQL, or H2 with Flyway enabled and ddl-auto=validate) so an entity<->migration mismatch fails in the 20-minute `server-tests` CI job instead of only in the 60-minute Playwright job's opaque "API never became healthy" timeout.

advisory.title: ResaleService.updateListing (price change + status-immutability guard + ownership) has zero test coverage
advisory.proof: ResaleServiceTest.java covers createListing, removeListing (incl. removeListing_notOwner_throwsNotFound), reserve, and markSold, but has no test for updateListing at all — neither the success path, the non-owner rejection, nor the SOLD/RESERVED immutability guard. ResaleControllerTest.java likewise has no PUT /api/resale/listings/{id} test. A regression in `requireOwnedListing` or the status guard (e.g. letting any authenticated buyer change another seller's asking price or flip a SOLD listing back to LISTED) would ship undetected, since every other mutating method in this service has an explicit ownership test and this one does not.
advisory.fix: Add ResaleServiceTest cases mirroring the existing removeListing ownership test: updateListing by the owner (price/condition/status change persisted), updateListing by a non-owner (rejected), and updateListing on a SOLD/RESERVED listing (rejected). Add a corresponding ResaleControllerTest PUT case.

advisory.title: StripeWebhookController's "invalid signature" test exercises a code path the real service never takes
advisory.proof: CheckoutServiceTest.handleWebhook_invalidSignature_throwsIllegalArgumentException (line 327) proves the real production code throws `IllegalArgumentException("Invalid Stripe webhook signature")` for a bad Stripe signature, and GlobalExceptionHandler.handleIllegalArgument (config/GlobalExceptionHandler.java:57-61) maps that to HTTP 400 — not 500. The controller test instead stubs a bare `RuntimeException` to hit GlobalExceptionHandler's generic 500 fallback (lines 86-90), asserting a status code the real invalid-signature path can never produce in production. No test exercises the real controller+service+exception-handler stack for an actual malformed/forged Stripe signature, so a regression that caused real signature failures to return 500 (or caused them to stop being rejected at all) would not be caught by this test.
advisory.fix: Mock `checkoutService.handleWebhook` to throw `IllegalArgumentException("Invalid Stripe webhook signature")` (matching the real exception type from CheckoutService) and assert 400, matching GlobalExceptionHandler's actual IllegalArgumentException->400 mapping; or better, replace the mock with the real CheckoutService + a mocked StripeCheckoutGateway so the controller-to-exception-handler chain is tested against the real exception.

advisory.title: No E2E coverage of the admin moderation flow or the 3D-generation lifecycle, despite the test inventory implying otherwise
advisory.evidence: test('edit product price', ...) ... test('delete product removes it from list', ...)
advisory.proof: No file under web/e2e/ references /admin or an admin moderation action (grep for "admin" across all e2e specs returns nothing), yet ADMIN is a privileged role with destructive actions (archive/remove products and posts, resolve reports) — those flows are unit/controller tested (AdminControllerTest, AdminModerationServiceTest) but never verified through the real UI end to end. Separately, web/CLAUDE.md's own E2E table claims designer-crud.spec.ts covers "image upload, 3D generation", but the actual file (read in full) only exercises create/edit/delete of a product's name and price — there is no image upload step and no polling for a generation status transition anywhere in the spec, so this production-critical flow has no E2E coverage at all (consistent with the structural gap that the worker container isn't part of the CI bring-up).

advisory.title: GuestAvatarController / GuestAvatarService (unauthenticated write path) has zero test coverage
advisory.proof: `find server/src/test -iname "*GuestAvatar*"` returns no results — confirmed against the actual test tree, not just the self-reported CLAUDE.md gap. This is an unauthenticated, public, write-capable endpoint (creates/reuses an internal `guest@iyae.internal` user and inserts `avatar_generation_tasks` rows) protected only by the generic per-IP rate limiter; a regression in the guest-user reuse logic (e.g. failing to reuse the single internal account and instead creating a new one per request) would go undetected by any automated test and could leave orphaned rows accumulating under normal anonymous traffic.

advisory.title: Catalog free-text search (`q`) uses a leading-wildcard LIKE with no usable index
advisory.proof: A `LIKE '%term%'` predicate cannot use a B-tree index in MySQL regardless of what's indexed (V2__indexes_and_constraints.sql only adds idx_products_status_category and idx_products_status_created, neither of which helps a leading-wildcard scan on name/description). Every search request therefore does a filtered scan of all PUBLISHED rows after the status predicate narrows it. At the current seeded scale (36 products) this is invisible; I could not confirm the production catalog size, so I can't say this currently breaks anything — flagging as a scalability gap that will show up as catalog size grows into the thousands, on the shop's search box specifically.
advisory.fix: Add a MySQL FULLTEXT index on products(name, description) and switch the `q` branch to MATCH ... AGAINST, or move search to a dedicated search index if the catalog is expected to grow past a few thousand PUBLISHED rows.

advisory.title: 3D-generation/avatar/rigging worker is a single serial process — no horizontal scale-out configured
advisory.evidence:
task = queue.claim_task()
            if task is not None:
                processed_any = True
                task_id = task["id"]
                product_id = task["product_id"]
                logger.info(f"Claimed model task {task_id} for product {product_id}")
advisory.proof: Each poll loop iteration claims and fully processes at most one model-generation task, one avatar task, and one rigging task, each synchronously end-to-end (network call to the provider, GLB validation, DB write) before looping again — there is no concurrency within the process. docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.prod.yml both declare exactly one `worker` service instance (the separate `rigging-worker` is also a single instance, gated behind the `rigging` profile). If a provider call takes on the order of a minute, 10 designers triggering generation within the same window queue strictly serially: the 10th request's task sits PENDING while the prior 9 complete, so its status poll (GenerationStatusController, 5s interval per web/lib/hooks/useGenerationStatus.ts) could show PENDING for several minutes. The underlying claim mechanism (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in worker/task_queue.py) is already safe for multiple replicas, so this is a deployment-topology gap rather than a code defect — I could not confirm how many designers submit generation requests concurrently in production, so this is flagged as a latency/availability risk under burst load rather than a confirmed outage.
advisory.fix: Run the `worker` service with multiple replicas (docker-compose supports it since task_queue.claim_task already uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, which is safe for concurrent claimers) when generation volume grows, or document the current single-instance ceiling so it's a known tradeoff rather than a surprise under a traffic spike.

advisory.title: JVM heap is explicitly capped in dev (384m) but left to container/host defaults in prod with no memory limit set
advisory.evidence:
server:
    build:
      context: ./server
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      DB_HOST: mysql
advisory.proof: docker-compose.yml:43 sets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-Xmx384m -Xms128m"` for the dev server only; grepping docker-compose.prod.yml for JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, mem_limit, or deploy.resources.limits on the server/mysql/web services returns nothing (the only `deploy.resources.limits` in the whole repo is on dev's optional `rigging-worker`, 1G/2 cpus). I could not confirm the actual production host's RAM or whether other containers (mysql, nginx, web) are similarly unbounded — so I can't say this currently causes an OOM — but it means prod JVM heap sizing is implicitly whatever 25% of host memory resolves to at boot, untested and undocumented, a different and unverified risk profile from the tightly-capped 384m dev config this repo otherwise relies on for day-to-day testing.
advisory.fix: Either set an explicit `-Xmx`/`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS for the prod server (matching whatever memory the host/container is actually provisioned with), or add a `deploy.resources.limits.memory` to docker-compose.prod.yml for the server/mysql/web services so the JVM's default heap-sizing (25% of visible memory when no cgroup limit is set) is based on a real number instead of the whole host's RAM.

advisory.title: Nine documented env vars are not passed into any container, so setting them in .env silently does nothing
advisory.evidence: | `ANALYTICS_DRAPE_DEPLOY_CUTOFF` | No | `` (empty) | ISO-8601 instant of the Phase 1-3 drape deploy; default split point for `GET /api/admin/kpis/drape-decision` pre/post comparison
advisory.proof: Neither docker-compose.yml nor docker-compose.prod.yml contains an `env_file:` directive, so .env performs variable substitution in the compose file only and never injects into containers -- any var not listed under a service's `environment:` block is unreachable. advisory.title: Body measurement client inputs allow values the server will always reject (no max, mismatched min)

advisory.title: Guest avatar generation shares one global user identity — cross-session avatar overwrite + unauthenticated IDOR on task status
advisory.proof: GuestAvatarController exposes `POST /api/public/avatar/generate` and `GET /api/public/avatar/status/{taskId}` fully unauthenticated (`/api/public/**` is `permitAll()` in SecurityConfig.java:48). Every call to GuestAvatarService.getOrCreateGuestUser() (lines 81-89) returns the SAME single `User` row keyed by `brandProperties.guestEmail()` — there is one guest identity shared by every anonymous visitor on the server. Consequently every `AvatarGenerationTask` created by `generateForGuest()` has the identical `user_id`, and the 'ownership' check at line 65 (`task.getUser().getId().equals(guest.getId())`) is vacuously true for every task that has ever been created by any anonymous visitor — it never rejects anyone. Worse, the worker writes the generated avatar to a path keyed by that same shared `user_id`: `worker/providers/smplx_provider.py:313-315,362` (`output_dir = .../avatars/{user_id}`; `glb_url: /assets/avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb`) and `smplx_stub_provider.py:234-256` do the same. Concrete production failure: Guest A submits measurements and gets task #101 (owner = shared guest id G). Guest B, an unrelated anonymous visitor minutes or hours later, submits different measurements and gets task #102 (owner is also G). B's generation completes and the worker overwrites `avatars/G/avatar.glb` with B's body mesh. A's own, already-completed result is now permanently destroyed (silent data loss), and if A polls `GET /api/public/avatar/status/101` again (or the frontend re-fetches the cached URL), A is served B's generated 3D body avatar as if it were their own. Separately, because the ownership check never actually discriminates between visitors, anyone can sequentially enumerate the auto-increment `taskId` (`@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)` on AvatarGenerationTask) with zero authentication and read the status/result/error of every guest avatar task the server has ever processed. No privileged precondition, no credentials, and no attacker sophistication beyond incrementing an integer are required — ordinary concurrent use of the advertised 'try without an account' flow reproduces the corruption on its own.
advisory.fix: Stop collapsing every anonymous visitor onto one shared `guest@iyae.internal` User row. Either (a) mint a per-session disposable identity (and have the worker key the output path by `task_id`, not `user_id`), or (b) at minimum change the SMPL-X/stub providers to write to `avatars/guest/{taskId}/avatar.glb` instead of `avatars/{user_id}/avatar.glb` so concurrent anonymous generations cannot collide, and bind `GuestAvatarStatusResponse` access to a per-generation secret (e.g. an opaque token returned from /generate) rather than a same-row comparison that is always true.

It positively rejects every task owned by a real authenticated user, so the unauthenticated enumeration of `taskId` cannot read any registered user's avatar task. No authenticated-user data is reachable through this endpoint.
2. `AvatarService.java:234` (`isGuest` by email) deliberately skips writing `User.avatarGlbUrl` for the guest row, so the collision cannot durably contaminate any user profile.
3. `RateLimitFilter.java:38` caps `POST /api/public/avatar/generate` at 3/min/IP. (GET status is unthrottled, so the enumeration itself is not rate-limited.)

Server Dockerfile has no non-root user, no built-in JVM memory ceiling, and no HEALTHCHECK
advisory.evidence:
FROM eclipse-temurin:22-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/build/libs/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
advisory.proof: The final stage never adds/switches to a non-root `USER`, so the JVM process runs as root inside the container — a defense-in-depth gap if any future RCE/arbitrary-file-write vulnerability is found in this app or a dependency. The ENTRYPOINT also bakes in no JVM heap bound (e.g. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage) of its own; the repo's only memory cap (`JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-Xmx384m -Xms128m"`) is supplied externally by docker-compose.yml and is documented in root CLAUDE.md as "dev docker-compose only" — docker-compose.prod.yml sets no JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and no container memory limit for the server service, so in production the JVM's default container-aware heap ergonomics are the only guard against a memory spike/leak taking down the shared host alongside MySQL/web/nginx. There is also no `HEALTHCHECK` instruction in the image itself (health checks exist only in the compose files), so the image has no self-contained liveness signal if run under an orchestrator that doesn't supply its own probe.
advisory.fix: Add a dedicated non-root `USER` in the final stage (chown the jar accordingly); set a conservative default heap bound directly in the ENTRYPOINT (e.g. `ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", "-jar", "app.jar"]`) so the image is safe even without an external JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS; add a `HEALTHCHECK` instruction as a baked-in fallback.

advisory.title: ImageUploader: stale upload can overwrite a newer selection, and an in-flight object URL can leak on unmount
advisory.proof: There is no guard against a second file being selected (via click or drag) while the first `uploadImage()` call is still in flight — `handleFile` has no request-id/AbortController. If the first upload resolves after the second has already started, its `.then` still runs and calls `onUpload(uploadedUrl1)` + `setPreviewUrl(uploadedUrl1)`, silently reverting the form's imageUrl back to the first (stale) file even though the user had already moved on to a second selection. Separately, the `URL.createObjectURL(file)` object URL is only revoked inside the same `handleFile` call's success/catch paths — if the component unmounts while the upload promise is still pending (e.g. the designer navigates away from the new/edit product page mid-upload), that blob URL is never revoked and leaks for the life of the SPA session.
advisory.fix: Track a request id/ref (or AbortController) per call and ignore a `handleFile` invocation's result if a newer one has started since; revoke the object URL (or at least guard the `setPreviewUrl`/`onUpload` calls) in a cleanup path if the component unmounts mid-upload.

advisory.title: bodyProfileVisibility is validated, persisted and exposed to clients but never read by any authorisation decision
